background.definition: Hirschsprung’s disease (HD) is a functional obstruction of the gut, where a segment fails to relax, thus preventing stool passage. It is caused by the lack of ganglion cells in the contracted segment of bowel.

list.listitem: One per 5000 live births.
Male to female ratio: rectosigmoid 4:1; total 2:1.
Thirty percent of HD cases associated with chromosomal abnormality or congenital syndrome; rest are isolated.
Malpractice risk for physician if failing to recognize HD presenting as enterocolitis.
Children with constipation account for 3% to 5% of all visits; HD should be ruled out.
Developmental failure of neuroblasts to migrate properly.
HD is associated with RET proto-oncogene mutations (50% familial, 20% sporadic).
Nerves cannot connect with enteric muscle for peristalsis. Missing ganglia occurs distally and extends proximally with variable lengths of bowel involvement.

Rectosigmoid involvement in 75% of HD patients. Involvement extends beyond the rectosigmoid in 10%, there is total colon involvement in 8%, entire bowel involvement in less than 1%, and ultrashort segment involvement (<5 cm) in less than 1%.

Rectal biopsy provides the definitive diagnosis (absence of ganglion cells and/or increased cholinesterase activity); suction rectal biopsy if less than 3 years of age and surgical full thickness biopsy of the rectum if older than 3 years. C
Anorectal manometry is used to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, which is absent in HD. C
Unprepped barium enema can detect the transition zone of the narrowed aganglionic segment into the dilated normal bowel. C
HD is associated with a variety of genetic disorders (). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive sweat chloride or genetic testing
Abnormal radiography, usually critically ill neonate
Family of disorders associated with intestinal dysmotility and normal anatomy
Usually has abnormal neonatal screening test
Associated with dehydration, infant appears ill
Resembles HD, diagnosis is based on rectal biopsy

list.listitem: Suspect HD if a child has a history of persistent constipation that is resistant to usual medical therapy. Also suspect HD if a newborn has not passed meconium within the first 24 hours of life (98% of normal full term infants pass meconium in the first 24 hours of life, compared with only 40% with HD).
Usual onset is at less than 3 months of age, but HD can be discovered at any age. Breast fed infants may not present until introduction of formula or purees.

Abdominal distention is a universal finding. May have feeding intolerance with bilious emesis associated with abdominal distention. Diarrhea, fever, constipation history, and abdominal distension signal possible enterocolitis as a complication.
Tight anus on digital exam is unreliable, especially after patient has had any rectal manipulation (digital exam, enemas, rectal temps, and so on).
Rare findings: prenatal history of obstruction; unexplained perforation of cecum or appendix.
See algorithm in .
Children younger than 3 years suspected to have HD should have a suction rectal biopsy, while those older than 3 years should have a barium enema or anal manometry.

Any of the following abnormal studies would warrant referral for full-thickness surgical biopsy: (1) suction rectal biopsy with absence of ganglion cells on routine histology and/or increased cholinesterase activity with special stain, Se 93%, Sp 100% (2) unprepped barium enema with caliber change between the dilated proximal ganglionic bowel and the small/normal caliber aganglionic bowel, Se 76%, Sp 97% or (3) anorectal manometry with lack of relaxation of anal sphincter on insufflation, Se 83%, Sp 93%.
Definitive diagnosis is based on a full thickness rectal/colonic biopsy specimen by an experienced pediatric surgeon (confirming absence of ganglion cells on histology).

Genetic testing should be strongly considered, as HD is associated with a genetic chromosomal trait in 12% of cases, with trisomy 21 being the most common. Other congenital anomalies are found in approximately 18% of patients, including cleft palate, gastrointestinal malformations, polydactyly, cardio-septal defects, and other craniofacial defects.
See algorithm in for suggested approach to evaluation.
Stabilize patient (IV fluids, assess nutritional status, NG tube if abdomen distended or vomiting, prophylactic antibiotics). C
Surgery is required to remove the aganglionic bowel and to connect ganglionic colon to rectum while preserving sphincter function. C
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover aerobic and anaerobic GI organisms. Specific antibiotic choice depends on local antibiotic resistance.
Very short segment HD may require laxative therapy.
Goals of surgery are to resect aganglionic segment, connect ganglionic, normally innervated bowel close to anus, and preserve sphincter function.
First identify most distal bowel with ganglia, usually with frozen section by pathologist, then decide either two stage (ostomy, then connection) or one stage (connection) procedure.

Choice of operation: (a) "Swenson"—resect rectum, end to end anastomosis just above sphincter, (b) "Duhamel"—leave rectum, attach colon in presacral space, (c) "Soave"—remove rectal mucosa, pull colon thru rectum, connect just above dentate line. Recent systematic reviews found that patients who underwent transanal endorectal pull-through (±laparoscopically) had fewer problems with soiling/incontinence (OR: 0.58; 95% CI: 0.37-0.90) and constipation (OR: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.30-0.81) compared with transabdominal surgery.

Potential post-op complications include: pelvic abscess, rectal stricture, anastomotic leak, cuff infection, wound dehiscence, recto-vaginal fistula, stomal prolapse/stenosis, enterocolitis. In one study of 34 children with HD following a stage one pull-through operation, 8 (24%) had early complications in the form of dehiscences of the anastomosis.
Long-term complications include: enterocolitis (up to 50%), constipation (up to 22%), fecal incontinence/diarrhea (up to 10%).
Transplantation of enteric nervous system stem cells, sourced from easily accessible postnatal gut, is investigated as an alternative treatment for HD.
Presurgical goal is to stabilize patient in anticipation of surgery. Assess fluid/electrolyte status and correct if necessary.
Assess nutritional status and initiate IV nutrition if severe. Place NG if abdomen is distended or patient is vomiting.
Perform serial rectal irrigation to decompress bowel if necessary. Very short segment HD may require laxative therapy.
Consult a pediatric surgeon for definitive treatment.
Obtain a genetics/dysmorphology consult to rule out chromosomal abnormality/syndrome (may require imaging).

Post-operative enterocolitis can lead to electrolyte imbalance, dehydration, and toxic megacolon. It usually occurs in first 2 years, but may occur up to 10 years later. Treatment of enterocolitis consists of rectal irrigation several times a day and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Post-operative constipation could be secondary to prolonged colonic transit times, stricture, or retained aganglionic segment. It is thought to be a factor precipitating enterocolitis.
Post-operative incontinence/diarrhea improves in first 6 months, with slow improvement over several years. Treatment of diarrhea includes dietary fiber and loperamide.

Postoperative complications are common. In one meta-analysis of studies of perioperative results following a single surgical procedure for patients with total colonic aganglionosis (the most severe form of HD), overall mortality was 1.9% and morbidity rates ranged from 10% to 64%; enterocolitis was noted in seven studies with a mean incidence of 22%.B
Fecal continence was poor in patients less than 15 years old, improving after adolescence. C
Post-operative outcomes: 64% "normal" stool habits; 90% of parents report moderate to very satisfactory outcome. B

In a meta-analysis of 68 cases of total intestinal aganglionosis (a rare form of HD), 11 patients (16.2%) died prior to surgical treatment, 25 patients (36.8%) only had jejunostomy, 20 (29.4%) had Ziegler’s myectomy-myotomy, and 12 (17.6%) received intestinal transplantation (ITx) or combined liver-intestinal transplantation (LITx). Forty-five patients (66.2%) died at ages ranging from 1 day to 8 years. Twenty-three patients (33.8%) were alive; the longest survivor was 10 years old after LITx.B

A cross-sectional cohort study comparing women with Hirschsprung's disease with population controls showed an increased proportion of patients reporting post-operative subfertility (1 year: 47% vs 21%, p=0.0008; 2 years: 27% vs 10%, p=0.004).B

Trisomy 22 (Cat-eye syndrome)
Neurocristopathies
MEN type 2A, familial medullary thyroid carcinoma
Neuroblastoma
Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine’s curse)
Waardenburg syndrome
Familial dysautonomia syndrome (Riley-Day syndrome)
Mowat-Wilson syndrome
Spritzen-Goldberg syndrome
Bardet-Biedl syndrome
Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome
